📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to upcoming ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

According to recent reports, in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem.

The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

Industry observers note that "What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," says lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena.".

Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure.

To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

Recent findings suggest that when laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

Industry observers note that "We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials.".

Light Responds to Direction and Polarization.

The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a latest type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

According to recent reports, "These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity.".

From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics.

The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover upcoming ways to control and study light.

  • Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site launched. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot update itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Sources indicate that freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Industry observers note that then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination users might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

In a recent development, the example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least notable layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

In a recent development, quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

It has been revealed that each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand proposal. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

According to recent reports, what is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

It has been revealed that is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for consumers. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

It has been revealed that how often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Sources indicate that do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

Industry observers note that how many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and people engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

In a recent development, the sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 players who used the Latest Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.

With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Fresh Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.

While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a New Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.

Unfortunately, getting into Vice City a few hours early appears to have come with an unexpected drawback.

As reported by IGN, Rockstar left out the ability to consume cocaine from your inventory in the Australian version of GTA 6, with Newly introduced Zealand reportedly receiving the same version.

In the international release, players can collect baggies of cocaine or skim some off larger bricks. Consuming cocaine through the item wheel gives players a supercharged stamina bar for roughly 30 seconds.

Australia’s video game classification rules allow depictions of illicit drug use but prohibit players from receiving gameplay benefits for taking them, even in games rated R18+.

Interestingly, Upcoming Zealand doesn’t have this same restriction, but testing by GTA BOOM found that the mechanic was also absent from its New Zealand playthroughs.

Players had already suspected GTA 6 was censored in certain regions before launch when dataminers discovered a roughly 700KB discrepancy in the Australian and New Zealand game files.

Unlike Xbox consumers who temporarily changed their console’s location, PS5 players who bought the New Zealand edition still own that regional copy even when playing on their regular account.

Luckily, those affected aren’t missing out on too much. Adrenaline can still be used to boost stamina and other stats, while scripted sequences involving cocaine remain intact.

Still, it’s a rather amusing twist that some of GTA 6‘s most impatient fans ended up with less content than those who waited a few extra hours.

#150796. MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

📅 22 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)

MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes.
  • Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a upcoming approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

Industry observers note that researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a upcoming approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

According to recent reports, "We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," claims Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

Chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller.

Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

Industry observers note that the team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

The physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

According to recent reports, to solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

Recent findings suggest that "The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates latest capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How says.

Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers.

The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can blueprint difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each upcoming flip under the proper conditions.

Sources indicate that "If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How notes.

It has been revealed that the researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate promptly enough for real-time flight.

A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

"The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

Experiments demonstrated that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

"This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up new opportunities for multimodal locomotion," notes Hsiao.

Sources indicate that the team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a new position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

"This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen says.

Toward Autonomous Flying Microrobots.

One major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

The team also aims to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

"For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a new control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," states Chen.

This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you’ve ever struggled with a tough math problem, you know how useful it is to think a little longer and work through it carefully.
  • According to recent reports, however, the recipe behind OpenAI’s reasoning models has been a well kept secret.
  • According to recent reports, besides performing as well or better than o1, the DeepSeek-R1 release was accompanied by a detailed tech report that outlined the key steps of their training recipe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you’ve ever struggled with a tough math problem, you know how useful it is to think a little longer and work through it carefully. OpenAI’s o1 model revealed that when LLMs are trained to do the same—by using more compute during inference—they get significantly better at solving reasoning tasks like mathematics, coding, and logic.

According to recent reports, however, the recipe behind OpenAI’s reasoning models has been a well kept secret. That is, until last week, when DeepSeek released their DeepSeek-R1 model and promptly broke the internet (and the stock market!).

According to recent reports, besides performing as well or better than o1, the DeepSeek-R1 release was accompanied by a detailed tech report that outlined the key steps of their training recipe. This recipe involved several innovations, most notably the application of pure reinforcement learning to teach a base language model how to reason without any human supervision. As shown in the figure below, making a powerful reasoning model is now very simple if you have access to a capable base model and a high-quality data mixture:.

However, the DeepSeek-R1 release leaves open several questions about:.

These questions prompted us to launch the Open-R1 project, an initiative to systematically reconstruct DeepSeek-R1’s data and training pipeline, validate its claims, and push the boundaries of open reasoning models. By building Open-R1, we aim to provide transparency on how reinforcement learning can enhance reasoning, share reproducible insights with the open-source community, and create a foundation for future models to leverage these techniques.

In this blog post we take a look at key ingredients behind DeepSeek-R1, which parts we strategy to replicate, and how to contribute to the Open-R1 project.

In a recent development, deepSeek-R1 is a reasoning model built on the foundation of DeepSeek-V3. Like any good reasoning model, it starts with a strong base model, and DeepSeek-V3 is exactly that. This 671B Mixture of Experts (MoE) model performs on par with heavyweights like Sonnet 3.5 and GPT-4o. What’s especially impressive is how cost-efficient it was to train—just $5.5M—thanks to architectural changes like Multi Token Prediction (MTP), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) and a LOT (seriously, a lot) of hardware optimization.

DeepSeek also introduced two models: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1, each with a distinct training approach. DeepSeek-R1-Zero skipped supervised fine-tuning altogether and relied entirely on reinforcement learning (RL), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to make the process more efficient. A simple reward system was used to guide the model, providing feedback based on the accuracy and structure of its answers. This approach helped the model develop useful reasoning skills, such as breaking problems into steps and verifying its own outputs. However, its responses often lacked clarity and were difficult to read.

It has been revealed that that’s where DeepSeek-R1 comes in. It started with a "cold start" phase, fine-tuning on a small set of carefully crafted examples to improve clarity and readability. From there, it went through more RL and refinement steps, including rejecting low-quality outputs with both human preference based and verifiable reward, to create a model that not only reasons well but also produces polished and consistent answers.

This all sounds great, but what's actually missing? Let's have a look at the missing pieces of the puzzle.

The release of DeepSeek-R1 is an amazing boon for the community, but they didn’t release everything—although the model weights are open, the datasets and code used to train the model are not 😢.

Industry observers note that the goal of Open-R1 is to build these last missing pieces so that the whole research and industry community can build similar or better models using these recipes and datasets. And by doing this in the open, everybody in the community can contribute!

As shown in the figure below, here’s our blueprint of attack:.

Note that we don’t want to stop at math datasets. There’s a lot of potential in exploring other areas, obvious one like code but also scientific fields such as medicine, where reasoning models could have significant impact.

#150794. Tech Report: Grand Theft Auto 6 review: Is this the best game ever?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1762 w)

Tech Report: Grand Theft Auto 6 review: Is this the best game ever?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dexerto

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 is the greatest open-world simulation ever created.
  • Vice City and the sprawling state of Leonida feel alive in ways no game has achieved before.
  • For all its spectacle, ambition, and criminal excess, GTA 6 is also a deeply human story about two people trying to survive together in a world determined to tear them apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 is the greatest open-world simulation ever created. It is a breathtaking recreation of modern America, with extraordinary attention to detail and unrivalled freedom.

Vice City and the sprawling state of Leonida feel alive in ways no game has achieved before. Every street, random character, and minor interaction contributes to a world that feels like it exists beyond the player. It’s a technical achievement that raises the bar for open-world games forever.

For all its spectacle, ambition, and criminal excess, GTA 6 is also a deeply human story about two people trying to survive together in a world determined to tear them apart. And it’s the combination of unprecedented scale and genuine emotional depth that makes Rockstar’s latest masterpiece so extraordinary.

Grand Theft Auto 6 follows the story of Jason and Lucia, both fighting to make a name for themselves in Leonida after falling on hard times. We meet the two characters years before the events of the game, as they come across each other in Vice City, both stealing the same car.

Beyond that, Lucia is searching for answers about her family, mainly her child, after she lost custody following a stint in prison. As well as trying to pay the bills while working for Brian Heder, Jason is trying to find himself after serving in the army.

To both get what they’re looking for, they must build their way up from petty thieves to significant-time bank robbers, all while dealing with what Leonida has to throw at them – it can get pretty wild, too.

It has been revealed that red Dead Redemption 2 was, for me, the greatest game ever made. Arthur Morgan’s story still remains my favorite in gaming, but what really made RDR2 special was the immersion. The Wild West felt totally real, making even the most ordinary activities enjoyable.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 takes everything that made RDR2 so impressive and brings it to a modern-day recreation of Florida. It feels as though Rockstar took the best elements of Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5 and amplified everything. The result is easily the most detailed open world ever created and quite possibly the best game of all time.

Leonida is absolutely packed with things to do. Whether you’re exploring the wilderness, discovering upcoming locations, encountering wildlife, or investigating mysteries, there’s always something to keep you occupied.

It feels like there’s a newly introduced random encounter waiting around every corner, and in true Rockstar fashion, the developer seems to have thought of just about everything.

Better yet, you’re rewarded for going off the beaten path. There’s so much to discover that simply taking a detour can be just as entertaining as progressing through the main story. This is a world that begs you to explore every inch of it, and it’s remarkably easy to lose track of what you originally set out to do.

The attention to detail is on another level, too. Even everyday objects like books get more care than you’d expect, weapons can be customized to your heart’s content, and there are countless interactions that reward players for their creativity.

For instance, there’s one encounter early on where an NPC is filling his truck with gas. Players can flick a lit cigarette in his direction, triggering a massive gas station explosion.

Visually, GTA 6 is spectacular and as incredible as Vice City looks, the surrounding areas are equally impressive. From the lighting and weather effects to the character models and animations, the hardware has been pushed to its limits.

There were so many times when I found myself driving down a highway or country road, simply marveling at the world. Towns feel genuinely lived in, complete with residential neighborhoods, commercial districts, strip malls, and a staggering number of interiors to explore. Even the traffic strikes a great balance between feeling authentic but never becoming so congested that it takes the fun out of driving.

The sheer amount happening on screen at any given moment is astonishing, especially considering the game’s graphical fidelity. There is a trade-off, however, with GTA 6 targeting 30 FPS on consoles. It’s disappointing not to have a smoother option, but given what has been accomplished with this world, it’s a compromise I’m willing to accept.

The sound design is superb, too. The bustling streets of Vice City are alive with traffic, conversations, and background noise, while the quieter areas of Leonida have their own distinct atmosphere. The radio stations are another highlight, with a fantastic selection of music that makes even a leisurely drive across the map an enjoyable experience in its own right.

Thankfully, GTA 6 is every bit as fun to play as it is to explore.

The missions are some of the best in a GTA game, with plenty of variety and outrageous moments that make the campaign a blast. There’s a great balance between the ridiculous situations we’ve come to expect from the series and the more serious story Rockstar wants to tell, without one ever undermining the other.

Recent findings suggest that much like RDR2, GTA 6 uses its early missions to introduce latest mechanics while gradually building toward something greater. There are some minor pacing issues in the opening hours, particularly with some of the more mundane tasks, such as fixing up the house for Lucia. It  takes its time establishing the world and its characters while allowing players to get a feel for how the game plays.

But like any great symphony, there’s a gradual build before the crescendo. Once the training wheels start coming off midway through Chapter 2, and especially in Chapter 3, GTA 6 begins to unleash its full potential.

Industry observers note that the revamped Wanted system, introduced relatively early on, adds an entirely newly introduced dimension to police encounters. Cops now take your appearance, the vehicle you’re driving, and whether you’re carrying weapons into account, forcing you to be much more conscious of your actions when trying to evade the law.

Industry observers note that playing as Jason and Lucia together is an absolute blast, thanks to some of the best teammate AI I’ve ever experienced in a game. If you’re using a suppressed weapon, your partner will do the same. You can even work together to line up synchronized headshots.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t some scripted interaction that requires a button press or an on-screen prompt like you’d find in an FPS campaign – the AI simply does it. Whether you’re controlling Jason or Lucia, it genuinely feels like you have a competent partner in crime and if you get caught or killed, it’s usually your own fault.

Perhaps my favorite aspect of the gameplay, though, is the focus on robberies. They’ve come a long way since GTA 4’s legendary Three Leaf Clover mission. We saw Rockstar expand on the concept with GTA 5 and again with RDR2, but GTA 6 takes it to another level entirely. Even an ordinary bank robbery can be as exciting as a meticulously scripted action sequence from a Call of Duty campaign or the Uncharted series.

Early on in Chapter 3, I robbed a jewelry store with both characters, broke into a safe, and made off with the loot, only to find myself in a heated police chase. I let my partner take the wheel while I tried to hold off the cops hot on our trail.

In a recent development, after putting some distance between ourselves and the police, but still not quite out of danger, I decided our best bet was to split up. I abandoned the main road, ran into the woods, and eventually stumbled across a farmhouse, where I stole another car and made my escape while my partner fenced the stolen goods.

What made the whole experience so memorable was that none of it felt like a carefully orchestrated mission. It was a situation I had got myself into and had to find my own way out of.

As you progress, you’ll acquire tools and skills that allow you to take a much stealthier approach, potentially pulling off robberies without the cops ever laying eyes on you.

This is fun in its own right, as completing a brilliant heist without getting caught genuinely makes you feel like a badass. However, the occasions when things don’t go according to plan make for some of the most riveting gameplay GTA 6 has to offer.

There’s a very real sense of jeopardy, too. With death resulting in the loss of all the cash you’re carrying, there’s a sudden rush of adrenaline when a robbery goes sideways and you’ve got a small fortune on the line.

And that’s before even getting into the campaign’s major action set pieces, which are among the finest Rockstar has ever crafted. The finale of Chapter 1 is a particular standout and comfortably ranks among the greatest missions I’ve ever played in a video game.

Story-wise, GTA 6 had enormous shoes to fill following on from Red Dead Redemption 2. Unfortunately, neither Jason or Lucia are written with as much depth and growth as Arthur Morgan or other key members of the Van der Linde gang. A lot of that comes down to Jason’s dialogue and his personality being quite dry compared to other GTA characters.

It has been revealed that dylan Rourke, who voices Jason, has his moments, and without getting into spoiler territory, there are some emotional moments where he nails it. However, he seems to have had a lot less to work with than Manni L. Perez, who helps make Lucia the more compelling of the two.

In a recent development, that mentioned, GTA 6’s MacGuffins do a fantastic job at keeping interest incredibly high and driving the main plot in between side missions. And we are comparing it to what I think is the greatest video game story of all time.

Leonida is the most impressive open world I’ve ever explored, the missions are fantastic, and Jason and Lucia deliver a fine story that lives up to the brilliant world around them.

Industry observers note that after more than a decade of waiting, Rockstar has delivered something truly special. GTA 6 isn’t just a worthy successor to GTA 5 and RDR2. It sets a new standard, not just for what open-world games can achieve, but for gaming itself.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is the greatest open-world simulation ever created. It is a breathtaking recreation of modern America, with extraordinary attention to detail and unrivalled freedom.

#150793. Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

📅 25 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1191 w)

Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software.
  • Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons.
  • "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," said Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a new way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

"We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," said Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.

A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction.

In a recent development, the strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

It has been revealed that quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

To fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The new results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

It has been revealed that "Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," remarked Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes.".

Why Non-Abelian Anyons Are Different.

According to recent reports, ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

It has been revealed that these anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a newly introduced type of particle with its own unusual rules.

"The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen noted.

Industry observers note that each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

Recent findings suggest that because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

Why Braiding Alone Was Not Enough.

In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

That experiment showed that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

"In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," stated Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough.".

Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations.

For the latest study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

Industry observers note that the S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

Industry observers note that by combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

"It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," mentioned Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers.

The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

In a recent development, the experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

According to recent reports, "So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen said.

Recent findings suggest that the next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on upcoming techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

#150791. This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

📅 01 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1120 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a latest optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos promptly and accurately.
  • According to recent reports, the key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light.
  • According to recent reports, the technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a latest optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos promptly and accurately. Unlike conventional systems that typically examine videos one after another using digital hardware, the UCLA technology can analyze 15 or more video streams at the same time.

According to recent reports, the key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light. This allows many videos to be evaluated simultaneously during a single optical pass rather than requiring each one to move separately through a conventional digital processing pipeline.

According to recent reports, the technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight. The researchers designed the optical AI system to serve as a high-throughput, attack-resilient first layer of defense for screening large amounts of manipulated and AI-generated video.

The Growing Challenge of Deepfake Detection.

Rapid improvements in generative AI have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, increasing the need for detection systems that are both accurate and capable of operating at large scale.

Many advanced deepfake detectors depend on enormous amounts of digital computation. A single analysis can require hundreds of billions of floating-point operations, and videos are often processed sequentially. As more content must be checked, both the processing time and energy requirements can rise proportionally.

Digital detection systems face another problem. Attackers can deliberately alter fake videos in subtle ways designed to confuse a detector and make manipulated footage appear authentic.

Professor Aydogan Ozcan and his UCLA team developed a hybrid digital-optical system intended to address both challenges.

A lightweight digital encoder first collects compact information about each video, including spatial, spectral, and temporal features. That information is transformed into a phase pattern and displayed on a programmable spatial light modulator.

It has been revealed that the resulting optical wavefront then travels through a free-space-based, passive optical decoder. At the other end, paired optical detectors directly produce an authenticity score for each video.

In effect, the system replaces a computationally demanding digital decoding network with a physical process that can handle many streams in parallel.

Nearly 98% Accuracy Across 15 Videos at Once.

In experiments using visible light, the processor examined 15 Celeb-DF videos simultaneously during each optical pass.

According to recent reports, it achieved an average detection accuracy of 97.79%, along with a sensitivity of 99.86% and a specificity of 95.72%. Sensitivity measures how successfully the system identifies manipulated videos, making the particularly high sensitivity notable for a screening tool designed to keep fake content from slipping through.

In a recent development, the 99.86% sensitivity translated to an average false-negative rate of ~0.14%. In other words, only a very small fraction of manipulated videos were incorrectly classified as authentic.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also pushed the system further by increasing its capacity to 18 videos in a single optical pass. Even at that level, average detection accuracy remained at 96.13%.

More Optical Layers Boost Performance.

The team found that the processor could also become more capable by increasing the physical depth of its passive optical decoder without substantially increasing energy use or inference latency.

When researchers added two optimized passive diffractive layers while testing more difficult deepfake manipulations, detection accuracy improved by ~6.8%.

These phase-only diffractive layers can be manufactured as passive, static optical structures/surfaces. They perform additional calculations through the diffraction of light, meaning they do not require additional electrical power while the system is performing an inference.

That approach could allow more sophisticated processing without the same energy costs that typically accompany larger digital neural networks.

Testing the System Against Google VEO-3 Videos.

It has been revealed that the researchers did not limit their experiments to conventional face swapping deepfakes. They also challenged the processor with videos produced using Google's VEO-3 model.

Newer generative AI systems can create footage that lacks many of the obvious artifacts associated with earlier deepfake technology, making them a more difficult target for detectors trained primarily on older forms of manipulation.

With only minimal fine-tuning, the optical processor achieved 94.80% accuracy and 97.61% sensitivity on previously unseen VEO-3 videos during experiments.

The results suggest that the approach could potentially adapt as generative AI technology continues to evolve.

A Deepfake Detector Designed to Be Harder to Fool.

The optical system also highlighted resistance to black-box adversarial attacks and provides inherent protection against white-box attacks.

It has been revealed that part of that security comes from the way the detector physically performs its calculations. Because some of the inference process takes place through diffraction, vital parameters of the optical model are effectively embedded within the hardware.

Industry observers note that those parameters can be difficult for an attacker to measure, reproduce, or reverse engineer. That makes reconstructing the detector and designing carefully tailored adversarial changes that can evade it considerably more difficult.

It has been revealed that the processor also continued working reliably when videos were affected by image noise, blur, JPEG compression, and experimental misalignments. According to the researchers, those results illustrate how optical computation could provide a more secure and dependable foundation for some artificial intelligence systems.

A First Line of Defense Against Deepfakes.

Rather than replacing sophisticated digital detectors entirely, the UCLA processor is designed to work as a highly sensitive first stage of a larger detection system.

Massive volumes of video could initially pass through the parallel optical processor. Content identified as suspicious could then be sent to more computationally demanding digital models for a more detailed final assessment.

Sources indicate that such a system could combine the strengths of both approaches. Optical processing could provide parallel operation, low decoder energy requirements, high sensitivity, resistance to adversarial attacks, and the ability to adapt to newer AI video generators, while conventional digital systems could provide deeper analysis when necessary.

The researchers say this combination could eventually be useful for large-scale content moderation, media authentication, surveillance, and other security-critical AI applications.

The authors of this work are Parnian Ghapandar Kashani and Dr. Shiqi Chen, who contributed equally, and Professor Aydogan Ozcan. The researchers are affiliated with the UCLA Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, the UCLA Bioengineering Department, and the California NanoSystems Institute.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we are launching the integration of four awesome serverless Inference Providers – fal, Replicate, Sambanova, Together AI – directly on the Hub’s model pages.
  • We’ve been hosting a serverless Inference API on the Hub for a long time (we rolled out the v1 in summer 2020 – wow, time flies 🤯).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we are launching the integration of four awesome serverless Inference Providers – fal, Replicate, Sambanova, Together AI – directly on the Hub’s model pages. They are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for JS and Python), making it easier than ever to explore serverless inference of a wide variety of models that run on your favorite providers.

We’ve been hosting a serverless Inference API on the Hub for a long time (we rolled out the v1 in summer 2020 – wow, time flies 🤯). While this has enabled easy exploration and prototyping, we’ve refined our core value proposition towards collaboration, storage, versioning, and distribution of large datasets and models with the community. At the same time, serverless providers have flourished, and the time was right for Hugging Face to offer easy and unified access to serverless inference through a set of great providers.

Just as we work with great partners like AWS, Nvidia and others for dedicated deployment options via the model pages’ Deploy button, it was natural to partner with the next generation of serverless inference providers for model-centric, serverless inference.

Here’s what this enables, taking the timely example of DeepSeek-ai/DeepSeek-R1, a model which has achieved mainstream fame over the past few days 🔥:.

Recent findings suggest that rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder & CEO at SambaNova: "We are excited to be partnering with Hugging Face to accelerate its Inference API. Hugging Face developers now have access to much faster inference speeds on a wide range of the best open source models.".

In a recent development, zeke Sikelianos, Founding Designer at Replicate: "Hugging Face is the de facto home of open-source model weights, and has been a key player in making AI more accessible to the world. We use Hugging Face internally at Replicate as our weights registry of choice, and we're honored to be among the first inference providers to be featured in this launch.".

This is just the start, and we’ll build on top of this with the community in the coming weeks!

The following example shows how to use DeepSeek-R1 using Together AI as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Together AI API key if you have one.

Install huggingface_hub version v0.28.0 or later (release notes).

Note: You can also use the OpenAI client library to call the Inference Providers too; see here an example for DeepSeek model.

And here's how to generate an image from a text prompt using FLUX.1-dev running on fal.ai:.

To move to a different provider, you can simply change the provider name, everything else stays the same:.

We expose the Routing proxy directly under the huggingface.co domain so you can call it directly, it's very useful for OpenAI-compatible APIs for instance. You can just swap the URL as a base URL: https://router.huggingface.co/{:provider}.

Here's how you can call Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct using Sambanova as the inference provider via cURL.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Together AI key you're billed on your Together AI account.

Recent findings suggest that for routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

This turn might not seem like that big of a deal to many of you... But in practice, this very clearly constitutes an abrupt cutting-off of the lion's share of the quasi-subsidized compute erstwhile accessible through HF.

Recent findings suggest that and though seldom overtly publicized as a core feature of the platform, that nonchalantly encouraging compute reservoir of yore (even if accessible only via select pockets, like Inference Endpoints) served for years as a kind of a phantom fertilizer, and a key one, for Machine Learning adoption, experimentation, and resource-strapped development – on par with other quasi-subsidized resources like Google Colab and ChatGPT . And it's entirely plausible that the availability of such resources en masse has been the single most notable prerequisite, as well as mandatory catalyst, for the continual evolution/democratization of open source ML specifically, whether in regards to utility or literacy or safety or any other oft-evoked marker, and in some large part the popularization of ML more broadly.

Of course, despite its qualitative obviousness, the impact of subsidized resources may be difficult, maybe impossible, to summate objectively or to quantify directly. After all they constitute a set of infrastructures the immediate production of which tends to assume forms that are often ephemeral, social – like practices, understanding, or values – and wherever concrete, often non-commercial, like open models, adapters, enthusiast contributions, articles, posts, etc. And by the markers of finance and markets, such productions may be deemed as having only a tangential value to, say, the capitalization potential of a given platform, all-the-while adding heavy and at times unforeseeably fluctuating costs upkeep.

Nonetheless, (and there are few better illustrations for this than ML) public access to subsidized resources persisting in open forms (non-transactional, nor overtly monetized, nor strictly delimited: like all public resources, services, libraries, spaces) simultaneously remains a key precondition for the economic and socio-cultural potential of the entire technological and research field as a whole, whilst continually stimulating the range and variety of forms this potential may ultimately assume.

According to recent reports, as recently as a year ago, I would avidly preach the merits of Huggingface to everyone I know: not only as the key extant firmament for humanist and democratized machine learning paradigms to emerge and thrive upon, but as a really-existing pre-figuration of a new form of society, one that may at last transcend the intertwined logic of alienation, separation, disparity, scarcity, disposability, amnesia, exploitation, and all the rest of it... That's what I used to associate with Huggingface. Nowadays though: I think of Huggingface, and my next thought is "$2.00".

In a recent development, I know that for resources or platforms to remain subsidized, such subsidies must come from someplace. And assuring reliable funding may be a challenge, especially these days. Nonetheless, I really believe that it would be a grave mistake long-term for HF to rely on standard transactional/commercial monetization sourced from its users, even to cover real costs (much less to extract surplus "value" from or for anyone). To best serve its role within the field, HF must instead move closer to operating as a non-profit, sourcing unconditional funding from elsewhere , with the assumption that it may always operate at a "loss", whilst playing a key role in the thriving and the dynamism of the field as a whole.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 has become the biggest game launch in livestreaming history, racking up 420 million hours watched in its first week as TheBurntPeanut and IShowSpeed led the charge.

After years of anticipation, GTA 6 finally released on November 19, with millions of players diving into Rockstar’s recreation of modern-day Florida.

The excitement extended to streaming platforms, with both Twitch and Kick giving away thousands of GTA 6 codes and Twitch even introducing upcoming advertising technology to help creators monetize their broadcasts.

Now, the numbers are in, and Rockstar has obliterated the competition.

According to Streams Charts, GTA 6’s 420 million hours watched nearly tripled the previous launch week record set by Valorant’s closed beta in April 2020.

Incredibly, GTA 6 surpassed the combined opening week viewership of Valorant, Elden Ring, Diablo IV, and Lost Ark. The game also set a launch record with 7.91 million concurrent viewers.

Twitch accounted for the most hours watched, followed by YouTube and Kick, with the latter two finishing remarkably close to one another.

TheBurntPeanut was the most-watched GTA 6 streamer during launch week, generating a staggering 11.43 million hours watched across his broadcasts, with YouTube accounting for the majority of that figure.

Meanwhile, IShowSpeed attracted the most concurrent viewers on a single channel as he approached the end of his 52-hour GTA 6 marathon, which saw the streamer break down in tears after completing the story without sleeping.

Spanish streaming star IlloJuan recorded the highest combined peak viewership across multiple platforms.

However, it wasn’t just streaming’s biggest names benefiting from GTA 6. Smaller creators also found themselves in the spotlight, including one streamer with zero viewers who received a surprise raid from Ibai.

In total, 1,056 channels broke their all-time peak viewership records while playing GTA 6, with 193 of them attracting at least 10 times their previous record audience.

With GTA 6’s multiplayer mode still to come and the potential for another generation of GTA RP content, Rockstar’s streaming dominance could be just getting started.

This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a upcoming kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.
  • The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.
  • Industry observers note that quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a upcoming kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.

The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.

Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors.

Industry observers note that quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.

Even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.

In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.

Recent findings suggest that their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.

A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates.

According to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.

Industry observers note that dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, remarked:.

"We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.

Sources indicate that "The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test.".

Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.

That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.

A Possible Role as Quantum Memory.

One longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.

In a recent development, dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, said:.

According to recent reports, "We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.

It has been revealed that "Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system.".

The Next Step Is Building a Prototype.

The team now prepares to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.

The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.

It has been revealed that the project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.
